result.summary: Glaucus, now a sea god, pursues the fleeing Scylla and tells her how eating a strange grass changed him from a fisherman into a god of the waters. She leaves without answering, and he angrily goes to Circe.

scenes.title: Galatea ends; Scylla returns
scenes.summary: After the argument summary of Glaucus's change, Galatea finishes her tale and the Nereids depart. Scylla comes back to the shore and cools herself in a secluded inlet.
scenes.stakes: Scylla is wary of the open sea and seeks safety in a lonely recess.

scenes.title: Glaucus pursues Scylla
scenes.summary: Glaucus appears, newly transformed, and woos Scylla, who flees to a headland. She watches him warily, and he declares himself a god, not a monster.
scenes.stakes: Scylla fears being caught by an unknown sea creature; Glaucus risks rejection.

place.name: a mountain ridge by the shore

scenes.title: Glaucus tells of his change
scenes.summary: Glaucus recounts how, as a fisherman, he saw his catch revive on a meadow's grass, chewed it, and plunged into the sea. The sea gods purified him and he awoke transformed.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus gives up his mortal life and home for an unknown new nature.

scenes.title: Scylla leaves; Glaucus seeks Circe
scenes.summary: Glaucus laments that his godhood means nothing if she is unmoved. Scylla leaves, and angry he goes to Circe.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus faces unrequited love and turns to magic out of rage.

notable_quotes.reason: Glaucus's bitter question: godhood is worthless without Scylla's love.

analysis.text: Transformation is sudden and accidental here, and it fails to win love, setting up Scylla's own cruel transformation.
Glaucus's tale draws on a Boeotian cult legend of a fisherman-turned-god at Anthedon.

legacy.text: The Glaucus and Scylla story inspired later poets and painters, including Renaissance and Baroque treatments.

fun_facts.text: Anthedon was a real coastal town in Boeotia, linked in ancient tradition with Glaucus.

language_notes.text: Anthedon was a coastal town in Boeotia, facing Euboea. It was traditionally Glaucus's home as a fisherman.
Proteus, Triton and Palæmon are sea deities. Palæmon was the mortal Melicertes, son of Athamas, who became a sea god.
The convoluted sentence says no livestock had ever grazed the meadow. The apostrophe to sheep and goats makes it sound like speech.
"New master" is wry: Glaucus owned the fish only briefly before they escaped back to the sea.
"Vouchsafed" means graciously granted. "Kindred honours" means honours due to fellow sea gods.
Purification by a charm repeated nine times and washing reflects ancient ritual cleansing. Nine was a common magical number.
Circe, the daughter of Titan (here the Sun, Hyperion's line), is the sorceress who will transform Scylla.

context_notes.text: Scylla is a nymph who avoids the sea gods and their advances, which is why she keeps to the shore.
Oceanus and Tethys are the Titan couple who rule the primal ocean, and they are the elders of the sea gods.

literary_notes.text: Scylla admires the very features that mark Glaucus as strange, yet she remains wary. Her ambiguity prefigures her rejection.
Glaucus interrupts his story with a parenthetical aside, assuring Scylla he is not inventing a tale, which makes his speech sound like a nervous suitor's.
Glaucus's repeated questions show that his divinity is worthless to him without Scylla's love, ending his speech in desperate pathos.
Glaucus's anger and his visit to Circe anticipate Scylla's tragic transformation into a monster.
